rows.name: toCVar
rows.plain: A contextual variable term from a de Bruijn index
rows.annotation: This is the variable branch of the term translation. To work out what it does on a particular occurrence, apply `fromIndex` to recover the binding marker and its reification first, then use `fromVar` to put that data inside the contextual term.

ties.name: fromVar
ties.plain: A contextual term from a packaged variable

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition turns the existential variable package into a contextual variable using the same saved marker and reification, matching this equation.
rows.name: fromVar
rows.plain: A contextual term from a packaged variable
rows.annotation: The paper's `MkVar` is Lean's `ProxyVar.PVar`. Matching it gives `fromVar` the saved marker together with the implicit `ReifyIndex` from its binding context to its use context. `STLCCtx.CVar` requires exactly those inputs, so `fromVar` can put them into the full term syntax while keeping the same guest type. The conversion changes the outer constructor. Computing the first-order index is a later step in `unembed`.

ties.name: toCVar
ties.plain: A contextual variable term from a de Bruijn index

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition agrees with the displayed composition $\operatorname{toCVar}=\operatorname{fromVar}\circ\operatorname{fromIndex}$. It first packages the index and then turns that package into a contextual variable.
rows.name: toCVar
rows.plain: A contextual variable term from a de Bruijn index
rows.annotation: The right-hand side runs from right to left. `fromIndex` turns a typed position into a marker and an instance. `fromVar` uses them to make a term of the index's guest type in the index's original context.

ties.name: isoL
ties.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term

rows.fidelity_note: The passage claims an isomorphism; this formal statement proves only that unembedding after contextualisation returns every original first-order term. The reverse equation is supplied by the other cited theorem.
rows.name: isoL
rows.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term
rows.annotation: This direction starts with first-order syntax and uses only instances built during `contextualise`. After `unembed` recovers the original term, it follows that two different first-order terms cannot acquire the same contextual representation. This direction uses no closed-world axiom.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage claims an isomorphism; this formal statement proves only that contextualisation after unembedding returns every original contextual term. Its proof uses the closed world assumption disclosed later in this subsection; the other cited theorem supplies the opposite direction.
rows.name: isoR
rows.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: This direction starts with an arbitrary contextual term, which can already contain a reification instance. The authors' Lean proof uses `closedWorld` (every supplied reification instance must be reflexive or a recursive extension) to ensure reconstruction from an index recovers that stored instance. Together with `isoL` it supplies the isomorphism under that assumption.

ties.name: indexIsoL
ties.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names an isomorphism of variable representations; this formal statement gives one direction: converting any index to a package and reifying it returns that index.
rows.name: indexIsoL
rows.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index
rows.annotation: Starting with a typed position makes the induction straightforward: each `Index.Pop` becomes one stored extension, which in turn reifies to one `Index.Pop`. The first-order round-trip proof (`isoL`) uses this equality at every variable leaf.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names an isomorphism of variable representations; this formal statement gives the reverse direction: reifying a package and converting the index back returns the original package. Its proof uses the closed world assumption.
rows.name: indexIsoR
rows.plain: Reifying and repackaging gives the original variable under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: Equality here concerns the whole variable package. Once reification has produced a position, rebuilding its package must recover the binding context and the stored instance as well as the marker. This is where the proof needs `closedWorld`.

ties.name: isoL
ties.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the displayed equation $\operatorname{unembed}(\operatorname{contextualise}(e))=e$ for every first-order term, in any context and at any guest type; its proof does not use the closed world assumption.
rows.name: isoL
rows.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term
rows.annotation: Read the expression from the inside out. Convert a first-order term to contextual syntax and read it back as first-order syntax. The equality holds with the same context and guest type, so a free variable's index is recovered along with the rest of the term.

ties.name: isoR
ties.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the displayed equation $\operatorname{contextualise}(\operatorname{unembed}(e))=e$ for every contextual term. Its proof uses the closed world assumption discussed immediately below, so equality of the displayed statements does not mean an assumption-free isomorphism.
rows.name: isoR
rows.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: Read the expression from the inside out. Turn a contextual term into a first-order tree and rebuild its contextual form. The equality is between contextual terms themselves, including their stored variable data. The proof recovers that data with `indexIsoR`, which uses `closedWorld`.

ties.name: indexIsoL
ties.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives the left-inverse equation discussed under this heading: reifying the variable package produced from any index returns the original index. It does not require the closed world assumption.
rows.name: indexIsoL
rows.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index
rows.annotation: The function `fromIndex` returns a variable package (`Var` in the paper), so the statement extracts its stored instance as field `.2` and its marker as field `.3`. Reifying with precisely that instance returns the original index. Field `.1` is the hidden binding context shared by the other two.

ties.name: indexIsoL
ties.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes proof by induction; the formal statement says that reifying the package produced from an index returns that index. The supplied proof does use induction on the index, but that proof method is not a separate theorem statement.
rows.name: indexIsoL
rows.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index
rows.annotation: In the `Index.Top` branch the two sides reduce to the same index. In the `Index.Pop` branch unfolding `fromIndex` and `weakenPVar` (`weakenCVar` in the paper) leaves a pop on each side. The induction hypothesis supplies equality of the indices inside those pops.

ties.name: indexIsoL
ties.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index

rows.fidelity_note: The passage explains how weakening and reification cancel at each Pop; the formal statement gives the resulting equality for the entire index. The supplied inductive proof follows this explanation, rather than stating a separate step-count theorem.
rows.name: indexIsoL
rows.plain: Reifying the packaged variable recovers its index
rows.annotation: Start with `Index.Pop Index.Top` in $[a,b]$. `fromIndex` creates the marker for $a$ in $[a]$ and stores an extension instance accounting for $b$. The equality in `indexIsoL` reifies with the instance extracted from that very package. It first gets `Index.Top` in $[a]$ and adds one `Index.Pop` in $[a,b]$. The proof inducts on the input index because each `Pop` adds exactly one such extension to the package.

ties.name: indexIsoR
ties.plain: Reifying and repackaging gives the original variable under the reifier axiom

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem gives the reverse variable round trip. Reify the saved marker with the package’s stored instance, then convert the resulting index back to recover the original package and its instance. The proof uses the closed world assumption introduced next in the paper.
rows.name: indexIsoR
rows.plain: Reifying and repackaging gives the original variable under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: This order reifies first, using the instance already present, and lets `fromIndex` build a fresh package from the resulting position. A custom instance could have chosen a different position of the same type. The proof invokes `closedWorld` to exclude that possibility and recover the original package.

ties.name: closedWorld
ties.plain: Axiom restricting index reifiers to reflexivity and context extension

rows.fidelity_note: The formal assumption says every reification instance is either the identity-context instance or a one-entry extension of another instance. This is the paper’s closed world condition, assumed here rather than derived from instance resolution.
rows.name: closedWorld
rows.plain: Axiom restricting index reifiers to reflexivity and context extension
rows.annotation: An instance is a record with a reification function. In a context $[a,a]$, a custom function could send the newest marker to the earlier $a$. `closedWorld` assumes that every supplied instance is the reflexive instance or is built by one application of `instReifyIndexSnoc` to a smaller instance.

ties.name: closedWorld
ties.plain: Axiom restricting index reifiers to reflexivity and context extension

rows.fidelity_note: The passage justifies the assumption by hiding a type class from users; the formal declaration simply assumes the two-case condition for every reification instance. It does not prove that a module boundary enforces that condition.
rows.name: closedWorld
rows.plain: Axiom restricting index reifiers to reflexivity and context extension
rows.annotation: Suppose a custom instance at $[a,a]$ sends the newest marker to `Index.Pop Index.Top`. Rebuilding from that position saves the marker in $[a]$, which differs from the input marker's context $[a,a]$. The authors propose hiding `ReifyIndex` so clients cannot supply such records. Their Lean proof uses the `closedWorld` axiom to exclude them.

ties.name: indexIsoR
ties.plain: Reifying and repackaging gives the original variable under the reifier axiom

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes the proof: case analysis on the reification instances, made possible by the closed world assumption. The formal statement is the resulting reverse round-trip equation; its proof does split on the two cases that assumption allows and recurses through the extension case.
rows.name: indexIsoR
rows.plain: Reifying and repackaging gives the original variable under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: For a marker bound in $[a]$ and used in $[a,b]$, the extension instance reifies it to `Index.Pop Index.Top`. Rebuilding drops the outer `Index.Pop` to recover the package in $[a]$, then reapplies `weakenPVar`. The general proof uses the axiom to put the instance into reflexive or extension form, so it can recover the step as well as the marker.

ties.name: isoL
ties.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names the variable case’s proof dependency; the formal statement gives the first-order term round-trip equation. Its variable case does use the index round-trip result, as the passage says.
rows.name: isoL
rows.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term
rows.annotation: The variable branch translates by `toCVar`, then applies the stored reification during `unembed`. This is exactly the operation in `indexIsoL`. Once it returns the same index, both sides are `STLC.Var` applied to it.

ties.name: isoR
ties.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names the contextual-variable case’s proof dependency; the formal statement gives the contextual term round-trip equation. Its proof uses the reverse variable round trip and therefore the closed world assumption.
rows.name: isoR
rows.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: The `STLCCtx.CVar` pattern binds an existing instance. After unembedding, the variable branch of `contextualise` only sees the resulting index. `indexIsoR` shows that its reconstructed package can be used to recover the input constructor with its original data.

ties.name: isoR
ties.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes the abstraction case’s use of function extensionality; the formal statement gives the contextual term round-trip equation. The supplied proof uses extensionality and the singleton marker to establish equality of the abstraction bodies.
rows.name: isoR
rows.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: The two abstractions contain host functions, so `funext` asks for equality on any input marker. The induction hypothesis recovers the original body at `ProxyTop.PTop`. Every input marker has that constructor, so the rebuilt function gives the original result at each input.

ties.name: isoL
ties.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term

rows.fidelity_note: The passage says that transferring proofs between the two representations relies on the round-trip results and so on the closed world assumption. This direction, unembedding after contextualisation returns the first-order term, is proved without that assumption; only the reverse direction uses it.
rows.name: isoL
rows.plain: Unembedding after contextualising recovers the first-order term
rows.annotation: When a proof is carried out on the first-order term, `isoL` guarantees that displaying it in contextual syntax and translating back does not change the first-order object. This direction uses the instances created by the forward conversion and needs no closed-world axiom.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement says that contextualising after unembedding returns the original contextual term, and its proof does use the closed world assumption, as the passage says. The passage concerns how proofs transfer between representations, which no formal statement here expresses.
rows.name: isoR
rows.plain: Contextualising after unembedding recovers the term under the reifier axiom
rows.annotation: Suppose a theorem starts with a contextual term $e$. A proof about its rebuilt form yields a proof about $e$ by rewriting with `isoR`, which uses `closedWorld` (the restriction to the two defined reification instance forms). This lets the metatheoretic proof use induction on first-order syntax and return to the contextual statement.
